newsitem.title: USA: FOMC retained tightening bias at Dec 17 session.
newsitem.headline: FOMC retained tightening bias at Dec 17 session.

text.p: Federal Reserve policymakers voted unanimously at their December meeting to keep monetary policy unchanged but agreed that interest rates were more likely to rise than fall in the future, according to minutes of the meeting released on Thursday.
The central bank's policysetting Federal Open Market Committee also agreed to keep a close watch on the U.S. stock market for its impact on consumer spending and the economy.
"The rise (in stocks) over recent years had been extraordinary and had brought market valuations to fairly high levels relative to earnings and dividends," the minutes said.

"In these circumstances," the minutes continued, "the members recognized the need to monitor with special care price movements in the stock market and asset markets more generally for their implications for consumer and other spending."
Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan threw global financial markets into turmoil in December when he warned of the economic dangers when "irrational exuberance" infects prices of stocks and other assets.
The minutes of the Dec 17 meeting were released a day after the FOMC again decided to hold rates steady. Minutes of this week's meeting will be released on March 27.

At the Dec 17 meeting, the FOMC voted to retain its bias toward a tighter monetary stance. "Inflation had remained subdued, but the members continued to view the risks as tilted toward increases in the future," the minutes said.

The Fed staff forecast prepared for the meeting in fact foresaw slightly higher inflation as measured by the Consumer Price Index in 1997 and 1998. The increase expected would have been somewhat larger if not for anticipated adjustments to the way the CPI is calculated, the minutes added.
The staff also saw the economy continuing to grow at a pace close to its long-term potential.
But the minutes made clear that the FOMC members did not see any great urgency for action against inflation.

"While the longer term risks might point toward rising inflation, there were reasonable prospects that inflation would remain contained, and any pickup in inflation, should it occur, was likely to be limited at least for a time," it said.
"Because the risks of waiting did not appear to be substantial at this juncture," it added, "anticipatory tightening was not yet called for."
"In the circumstances, the members concluded that watchful waiting remained the prudent course for policy as they continued to assess ongoing developments," the minutes said.
Still, FOMC members agreed that their next policy move was "more likely to be in the direction of some firming than toward easing."
Some members also stressed the importance of acting promptly to counter any tendency for price inflation to rise and for higher inflation expectations to seep into financial markets and the economy.

In assessing the outlook for the economy, the FOMC said it expected the expansion to be supported by consumer spending, smaller though still sizeable gains in business investment and by slight improvement in nonresidential construction spending.
However, fiscal policy and the foreign sector would act to restrain growth, despite an expected acceleration in exports.

Some FOMC members voiced optimism about the prospects for a balanced budget deal between the Clinton administration and Congress and noted that such an agreement would benefit financial markets and boost consumer and business confidence.
That would tend to offset, at least in part, any drag on the economy from reduced government spending, the members noted.

On the inflation front, the FOMC was particularly focused on rising wages and worker benefits. It said an upturn in the core inflation rate "seemed quite possible at some point in the absence of some easing of pressures in labor markets."

But it added that there was a great deal of uncertainty about the outlook for inflation given that wages have risen significantly less than would have been expected with such low national unemployment.
